questions.title: Why is the sequence importance ratio in GSPO length-normalized?
questions.question_body: In the GSPO paper, the importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$ is defined as the sequence likelihood ratio raised to the power of $1/|y_i|$, specifically: $s_{i}(\theta) = \left( \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta\text{old}} (y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}}$. I'm confused about why this length normalization is necessary. In standard importance sampling, the weight is usually just the ratio of the two distributions. Wouldn't using the raw sequence likelihood ratio be more theoretically sound, and why does the authors' claim that this controls the numerical range matter for the clipping mechanism?

questions.title: Why is the GRPO objective considered 'ill-posed' for long sequences?
questions.question_body: The authors argue that GRPO is unstable because it applies importance weights $w_{i,t}(\theta)$ at each token position. They claim this introduces high-variance noise that accumulates over long sequences, leading to 'catastrophic model collapse'. I understand that importance sampling is meant to correct distributional mismatch, but I don't understand why applying the weight at the token level specifically fails whereas applying it at the sequence level succeeds. What exactly is the 'misapplication' of importance sampling happening in GRPO?

questions.title: Understanding the stop-gradient ($\mathrm{sg}$) operation in GSPO-token
questions.question_body: In the GSPO-token variant, the ratio $s_{i,t}(\theta)$ is defined as $\mathrm{sg} [ s_{i}(\theta) ] \cdot \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) }{ \mathrm{sg} [ \pi_{\theta} (y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) ] }$. The paper states that this is numerically equal to $s_i(\theta)$. If the numerical value is the same, why use this complex formulation involving $\mathrm{sg}$ (stop-gradient/detach) operations? Does this change how the gradients are backpropagated compared to simply using $s_i(\theta)$ in the objective function?

questions.title: How does GSPO's gradient weighting differ from GRPO's in practice?
questions.question_body: Looking at the gradient analysis in Section 4.2, it seems that in GRPO, each token's log-likelihood gradient is weighted by its specific token-level importance ratio $w_{i,t}(\theta)$. In GSPO, every token in the sequence is weighted by the same sequence-level ratio $s_i(\theta)$. If we are trying to optimize the overall sequence, why does weighting all tokens equally based on the sequence average lead to more stability than weighting them individually based on their specific contribution to the shift?

questions.title: How does GSPO resolve 'expert-activation volatility' in MoE models without Routing Replay?
questions.question_body: The paper explains that in MoE models, GRPO fails because different experts might be activated for the same token after a policy update, making the token-level ratio $w_{i,t}(\theta)$ fluctuate wildly. The authors claim GSPO resolves this because it is 'not sensitive to the individual token likelihood'. However, the sequence likelihood $\pi_\theta(y|x)$ is just the product of individual token likelihoods $\prod \pi_\theta(y_t | x, y_{<t})$. If the individual token likelihoods are fluctuating due to different expert activations, wouldn't the product (the sequence likelihood) also fluctuate? I don't see how GSPO is fundamentally 'insensitive' to this volatility if the underlying components are still the same token-level probabilities.
